items.stem: Social cost is equal to
items.answer: private cost plus external cost
items.markingKey: SC = PC + EC.

items.stem: Explain why the existence of external costs means that the price mechanism leads to over-production.
items.answer: Producers base decisions on private costs; the price does not include the external cost, so output is where MPC = MSB, beyond the social optimum where MSC = MSB.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: private decisions ignore EC; 1 mark: MPC < MSC; 1 mark: output too high [3]

items.stem: Distinguish between private benefits and external benefits, using education as an example.
items.answer: Private benefits go to the student (higher earnings, satisfaction); external benefits go to third parties (more productive workforce, lower crime, higher tax revenue).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each with example [2]

items.stem: A student in Calvania gains a private benefit of $110 thousand from a training course and society gains an external benefit of $5 thousand. Calculate the social benefit.
items.answer: $115 thousand
items.markingKey: SB = PB + EB = 110 + 5 = $115 thousand.

items.stem: A factory in Lima producing restaurant meals has a private cost of $80 per unit. Pollution imposes a cost of $10 per unit on local residents. Calculate the social cost per unit.

Extract: A coal-fired power station near Riyadh in Korvia produces 500 thousand units a year at a private cost of $60 per unit. Scientists estimate that air and water pollution impose an external cost of $20 per unit on local farms and residents. The government is considering a tax. (a) Explain why the government might set a tax of $20 per unit. (b) Explain two difficulties in measuring the external cost.
items.answer: (a) A tax equal to the marginal external cost internalises the externality, shifting MPC up to MSC so the firm produces the socially optimal output. (b) Health and environmental damage have no market price (shadow pricing needed); effects are spread over many people and time; causation uncertain.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark internalise; 1 mark output falls to optimum [2] (b) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: An external benefit is
options: a benefit received by the buyer
the profit made by the seller
a benefit enjoyed by a third party who is not directly involved in the transaction
a benefit paid for by the government
items.answer: a benefit enjoyed by a third party who is not directly involved in the transaction
items.markingKey: Externality: spillover effect on third parties not reflected in the price.

items.stem: Explain why it is difficult to place a monetary value on external costs.
items.answer: Many effects (health, noise, loss of biodiversity) have no market price, they are spread over many people and over time, and the cause-and-effect link may be uncertain, so shadow prices must be estimated.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: no market price; 1 mark: uncertainty/many parties [2]

items.stem: Production of paper causes pollution with a constant marginal external cost of $30 per unit. Output (000 tonnes): 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6; MPB ($): 100, 88, 76, 64, 52, 40; MPC ($): 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80. Identify (a) the free-market output and (b) the socially optimal output. (c) Explain the difference.
items.answer: (a) 4 thousand tonnes (b) 2 thousand tonnes (c) The market ignores the external cost, so over-produces by 2 thousand tonnes.
items.markingKey: (a) largest output where MPB ≥ MPC: 4 [1]; (b) MSC = MPC + 30: 60, 70, 80, 90, 100, 110; largest output where MPB ≥ MSC: 2 [2]; (c) external cost ignored → over-production [1].

items.stem: Production of cement causes pollution with a constant marginal external cost of $22 per unit. Output (000 tonnes): 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6; MPB ($): 100, 88, 76, 64, 52, 40; MPC ($): 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80. Identify (a) the free-market output and (b) the socially optimal output. (c) Explain the difference.
items.answer: (a) 4 thousand tonnes (b) 3 thousand tonnes (c) The market ignores the external cost, so over-produces by 1 thousand tonnes.
items.markingKey: (a) largest output where MPB ≥ MPC: 4 [1]; (b) MSC = MPC + 22: 52, 62, 72, 82, 92, 102; largest output where MPB ≥ MSC: 3 [2]; (c) external cost ignored → over-production [1].

items.stem: Residents of Jakarta complain about traffic noise and air pollution from a new logistics centre. (a) Explain the difference between private costs, external costs and social costs. (b) Assess whether the free market will produce too much of goods that create external costs.
items.answer: (a) Explanation of the theory (with a described diagram where relevant), drawing on: Producers/consumers ignore external costs, so MPC < MSC and output exceeds the social optimum. (b) Case for the view: Producers/consumers ignore external costs, so MPC < MSC and output exceeds the social optimum. Case against / evaluation: Size of the externality and elasticity; Coase bargaining when property rights are clear and few parties; some producers self-regulate for reputation; measurement difficulties. Conclusion: a judgement on the conditions under which the view holds.
items.markingKey: (a) Knowledge and understanding of the theory, clear analytical chain; diagram described accurately with labelled axes and curves. (b) Analysis of arguments for and against; evaluation reaches a justified conclusion that weighs the conditions under which the claim holds. Top level needs a judgement, not just a summary.

items.stem: In a diagram of a negative production externality, the welfare loss is shown by the triangle between
options: the price and the MPC curve up to the social optimum
MSC and MSB from the social optimum to the market output
MPC and MPB below the market output
items.answer: MSC and MSB from the social optimum to the market output
items.markingKey: DWL: area between MSC and MSB (= MPB) over the units produced beyond the social optimum.

items.stem: With the aid of a diagram, explain the welfare loss caused by a negative externality in production.
items.answer: Diagram: price/cost on vertical axis, quantity horizontal. MPB = MSB downward sloping; MPC upward sloping; MSC above MPC by the marginal external cost. Market output Q1 where MPC = MSB; social optimum Q* where MSC = MSB, at a higher price. Between Q* and Q1, MSC > MSB: the triangle between MSC and MSB from Q* to Q1 is the deadweight welfare loss.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: correctly drawn curves; 1 mark: Q1 and Q*; 1 mark: identifies welfare loss area; 1 mark: explanation that MSC > MSB for those units [4]

items.stem: With the aid of a diagram, explain why a merit good with positive consumption externalities is under-consumed.
items.answer: Diagram: MPB below MSB; MPC = MSC. Market output Q1 where MPB = MPC; optimum Q* where MSB = MSC is larger. Units between Q1 and Q* have MSB > MSC but are not consumed: welfare loss triangle between MSB and MSC from Q1 to Q*.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: MSB above MPB; 1 mark: Q1 < Q*; 1 mark: welfare loss triangle; 1 mark: reasoning [4]

items.stem: In the market for bicycle commuting, MPB: P = 60 − 1Q and MPC = MSC: P = 20 + 1Q, where P is in $ and Q in thousand units. Consumption gives a constant marginal external benefit of $6. Calculate the free-market output and the socially optimal output.
items.answer: 20 thousand and 23 thousand

items.stem: In the market for plastic packaging, MPB = MSB: P = 80 − 1Q and MPC: P = 20 + 2Q, where P is in $ and Q in thousand units. Production imposes a constant marginal external cost of $9. Calculate the free-market output, the socially optimal output and price, and the deadweight welfare loss.
items.answer: Market output 20 thousand; social optimum 17 thousand at P = $63; welfare loss = $13.5 thousand.

items.stem: In the market for fertiliser, MPB = MSB: P = 90 − 1Q and MPC: P = 10 + 1Q, where P is in $ and Q in thousand units. Production imposes a constant marginal external cost of $4. Calculate the free-market output, the socially optimal output and price, and the deadweight welfare loss.
items.answer: Market output 40 thousand; social optimum 38 thousand at P = $52; welfare loss = $4 thousand.

items.stem: Extract: A chemical plant near Cairo in Zentara produces 400 thousand units a year at a private cost of $60 per unit. Scientists estimate that air and water pollution impose an external cost of $10 per unit on local farms and residents. The government is considering a tax. (a) Calculate the social cost per unit and the total external cost per year. (b) Explain two difficulties in measuring the external cost.
items.answer: (a) $70 per unit; $4m a year (b) Health and environmental damage have no market price (shadow pricing needed); effects are spread over many people and time; causation uncertain.

items.stem: Extract: A paper mill near Dubai in Quentara produces 400 thousand units a year at a private cost of $80 per unit. Scientists estimate that air and water pollution impose an external cost of $25 per unit on local farms and residents. The government is considering a tax. (a) With the aid of a diagram, explain why the free market leads to a welfare loss. (b) Explain why the government might set a tax of $25 per unit.
items.answer: (a) MSC lies above MPC by the external cost; market output where MPC = MSB exceeds the optimum where MSC = MSB; welfare loss triangle between MSC and MSB over the excess output. (b) A tax equal to the marginal external cost internalises the externality, shifting MPC up to MSC so the firm produces the socially optimal output.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark curves; 1 mark outputs; 1 mark welfare loss area [3] (b) 1 mark internalise; 1 mark output falls to optimum [2]

items.stem: A positive consumption externality means that
options: MSB is greater than MPB, so the good is under-consumed
items.answer: MSB is greater than MPB, so the good is under-consumed
items.markingKey: External benefits make MSB > MPB; free-market output where MPB = MSC is below the optimum.

items.stem: Explain why the welfare loss from a negative externality is not the whole of the external cost.
items.answer: Only units produced beyond the social optimum cause a net loss; external costs on units up to the optimum are outweighed by net benefits, so the welfare loss is the triangle, not the full area between MSC and MPC.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: only excess units; 1 mark: triangle vs full area [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) With the aid of a diagram, explain the welfare loss caused by a negative externality in production. (b) Explain why the welfare loss from a negative externality is not the whole of the external cost.

Market output Q1 where MPC = MSB; social optimum Q* where MSC = MSB, at a higher price. Between Q* and Q1, MSC > MSB: the triangle between MSC and MSB from Q* to Q1 is the deadweight welfare loss. (b) Only units produced beyond the social optimum cause a net loss; external costs on units up to the optimum are outweighed by net benefits, so the welfare loss is the triangle, not the full area between MSC and MPC.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: correctly drawn curves; 1 mark: Q1 and Q*; 1 mark: identifies welfare loss area; 1 mark: explanation that MSC > MSB for those units [4] (b) 1 mark: only excess units; 1 mark: triangle vs full area [2]

items.stem: In the market for coal-fired electricity, MPB = MSB: P = 110 − 1Q and MPC: P = 10 + 1Q, where P is in $ and Q in thousand units. Production imposes a constant marginal external cost of $6. Calculate the free-market output and the socially optimal output.
items.answer: 50 thousand and 47 thousand

items.stem: A chemical works in Mexico City discharges waste into a river used by fishing communities. (a) With the aid of a diagram, explain how a negative production externality causes a misallocation of resources. (b) To what extent do you agree that externalities provide the strongest case for government intervention in markets?
items.answer: (a) Explanation of the theory (with a described diagram where relevant), drawing on: Externalities create welfare losses that markets cannot correct alone; taxes, subsidies, regulation. (b) Case for the view: Externalities create welfare losses that markets cannot correct alone; taxes, subsidies, regulation. Case against / evaluation: Other failures (public goods, monopoly, information) also justify intervention; government failure; measurement problems. Conclusion: a judgement on the conditions under which the view holds.
items.markingKey: (a) Knowledge and understanding of the theory, clear analytical chain; diagram described accurately with labelled axes and curves. (b) Analysis of arguments for and against; evaluation reaches a justified conclusion that weighs the conditions under which the claim holds. Top level needs a judgement, not just a summary.

items.stem: Vaccination rates in Kestria have fallen below the level needed to protect the whole population. Assess whether the welfare loss from positive externalities is less serious than that from negative externalities.
items.answer: Arguments for: Positive externalities: under-consumption, welfare loss triangle between MSB and MSC; negative: over-production and harm to third parties. Arguments against / evaluation: Size of loss depends on elasticities and size of externality, not its sign; education and vaccination losses can be large; long-run effects; equity aspects of who bears the cost. Conclusion: a supported judgement that depends on the conditions identified.
items.markingKey: Knowledge and analysis (about 60%): accurate theory, logical chains of reasoning and a relevant diagram described with axes, curves and shifts. Evaluation (about 40%): considers both sides, the assumptions and the context, and reaches a justified conclusion.

items.stem: Cost-benefit analysis is mainly used to
options: set the price of a public good
appraise public projects by comparing all social costs and benefits
items.answer: appraise public projects by comparing all social costs and benefits
items.markingKey: CBA weighs social (private + external) costs and benefits, usually discounted to present values.

items.stem: Explain two limitations of cost-benefit analysis.
items.answer: Valuing intangibles (noise, lives, environment) relies on uncertain shadow prices; choice of discount rate can change the result; forecasting future benefits is uncertain; distribution of costs and benefits is ignored by a simple total.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each limitation identified, 1 mark each explained [4]

items.stem: Explain why the choice of discount rate matters in a cost-benefit analysis of a long-term project.
items.answer: A higher discount rate reduces the present value of benefits far in the future more than near-term costs, so long-lived projects (e.g. flood defences) look less worthwhile; a low rate favours them.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: higher rate lowers PV of distant flows; 1 mark: effect on decision [2]

items.stem: The government of Jovania is appraising a new bypass road. The initial cost is $150m (now). Expected social benefits are $80m in year 1, $70m in year 2, $40m in year 3, with external costs of $5m each year. The discount rate is 4%. Calculate the present value of the net benefit in year 1.

The government of Marvona is appraising a hospital extension. The initial cost is $300m (now). Expected social benefits are $70m in year 1, $100m in year 2, $40m in year 3, with external costs of $15m each year. The discount rate is 8%. Calculate the net present value and the benefit–cost ratio, and state whether the project should go ahead.
items.answer: NPV = −$156.35m; benefit–cost ratio = 0.48; reject on these figures.

items.answer: (a) $105 per unit; $12.5m a year (b) A tax equal to the marginal external cost internalises the externality, shifting MPC up to MSC so the firm produces the socially optimal output.

items.stem: Explain how time savings from a new road might be valued in a cost-benefit analysis.
items.answer: By estimating hours saved per journey × number of journeys × a shadow price per hour (e.g. average wage for work time, a lower value for leisure).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: hours × journeys; 1 mark: shadow price per hour [2]

items.stem: A proposed airport runway near Muscat is being appraised. Classify each of the following as a private or external cost or benefit: (i) fares paid by passengers, (ii) noise for local residents, (iii) jobs created in local hotels, (iv) construction costs paid by the airport operator.
items.answer: (i) private benefit to passengers (revenue to airline), (ii) external cost, (iii) external benefit, (iv) private cost.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each correct classification [4]

items.stem: The government of Merania is appraising a sports stadium. The initial cost is $150m (now). Expected social benefits are $50m in year 1, $60m in year 2, $70m in year 3, $100m in year 4, with external costs of $10m each year. The discount rate is 3%. Calculate the net present value and the benefit–cost ratio, and state whether the project should go ahead. Explain one reason why the decision might still be controversial.
items.answer: NPV = $70.84m; benefit–cost ratio = 1.47; go ahead on these figures. Shadow prices and forecasts are uncertain and the discount rate is a value judgement; those who bear the external costs may not be those who benefit.
items.markingKey: PV of net benefits: year 1: 40/1.03^1 = 38.83; year 2: 50/1.03^2 = 47.13; year 3: 60/1.03^3 = 54.91; year 4: 90/1.03^4 = 79.96 [2]. Sum = 220.84; NPV = 220.84 − 150 = 70.84 [1]; BCR = 1.47 [1]; decision [1]. Valid limitation (uncertainty, distribution, discount rate) [1].

items.markingKey: Producers ignore external costs: MPC < MSC, so output where MPC = MSB exceeds output where MSC = MSB.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why the existence of external costs means that the price mechanism leads to over-production. (b) Explain why it is difficult to place a monetary value on external costs.
items.answer: (a) Producers base decisions on private costs; the price does not include the external cost, so output is where MPC = MSB, beyond the social optimum where MSC = MSB. (b) Many effects (health, noise, loss of biodiversity) have no market price, they are spread over many people and over time, and the cause-and-effect link may be uncertain, so shadow prices must be estimated.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: private decisions ignore EC; 1 mark: MPC < MSC; 1 mark: output too high [3] (b) 1 mark: no market price; 1 mark: uncertainty/many parties [2]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Distinguish between private benefits and external benefits, using education as an example. (b) Explain why the existence of external costs means that the price mechanism leads to over-production.
items.answer: (a) Private benefits go to the student (higher earnings, satisfaction); external benefits go to third parties (more productive workforce, lower crime, higher tax revenue). (b) Producers base decisions on private costs; the price does not include the external cost, so output is where MPC = MSB, beyond the social optimum where MSC = MSB.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each with example [2] (b) 1 mark: private decisions ignore EC; 1 mark: MPC < MSC; 1 mark: output too high [3]

items.stem: Production of cement causes pollution with a constant marginal external cost of $36 per unit. Output (000 tonnes): 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6; MPB ($): 90, 78, 66, 54, 42, 30; MPC ($): 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70. Identify (a) the free-market output and (b) the socially optimal output. (c) Explain the difference.
items.answer: (a) 4 thousand tonnes (b) 2 thousand tonnes (c) The market ignores the external cost, so over-produces by 2 thousand tonnes.
items.markingKey: (a) largest output where MPB ≥ MPC: 4 [1]; (b) MSC = MPC + 36: 56, 66, 76, 86, 96, 106; largest output where MPB ≥ MSC: 2 [2]; (c) external cost ignored → over-production [1].

items.stem: A student in Fendaria gains a private benefit of $70 thousand from a training course and society gains an external benefit of $20 thousand. Calculate the social benefit.
items.answer: $90 thousand
items.markingKey: SB = PB + EB = 70 + 20 = $90 thousand.

items.stem: Residents of Nairobi complain about traffic noise and air pollution from a new logistics centre. (a) Explain the difference between private costs, external costs and social costs. (b) To what extent do you agree that the free market will produce too much of goods that create external costs?
items.answer: (a) Explanation of the theory (with a described diagram where relevant), drawing on: Producers/consumers ignore external costs, so MPC < MSC and output exceeds the social optimum. (b) Case for the view: Producers/consumers ignore external costs, so MPC < MSC and output exceeds the social optimum. Case against / evaluation: Size of the externality and elasticity; Coase bargaining when property rights are clear and few parties; some producers self-regulate for reputation; measurement difficulties. Conclusion: a judgement on the conditions under which the view holds.
items.markingKey: (a) Knowledge and understanding of the theory, clear analytical chain; diagram described accurately with labelled axes and curves. (b) Analysis of arguments for and against; evaluation reaches a justified conclusion that weighs the conditions under which the claim holds. Top level needs a judgement, not just a summary.

items.stem: A positive production externality shifts which curve below the private cost curve?
items.answer: Marginal social cost
items.markingKey: External benefits in production mean MSC < MPC.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why the welfare loss from a negative externality is not the whole of the external cost. (b) With the aid of a diagram, explain why a merit good with positive consumption externalities is under-consumed.
items.answer: (a) Only units produced beyond the social optimum cause a net loss; external costs on units up to the optimum are outweighed by net benefits, so the welfare loss is the triangle, not the full area between MSC and MPC. (b) Diagram: MPB below MSB; MPC = MSC. Market output Q1 where MPB = MPC; optimum Q* where MSB = MSC is larger. Units between Q1 and Q* have MSB > MSC but are not consumed: welfare loss triangle between MSB and MSC from Q1 to Q*.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: only excess units; 1 mark: triangle vs full area [2] (b) 1 mark: MSB above MPB; 1 mark: Q1 < Q*; 1 mark: welfare loss triangle; 1 mark: reasoning [4]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) With the aid of a diagram, explain why a merit good with positive consumption externalities is under-consumed. (b) With the aid of a diagram, explain the welfare loss caused by a negative externality in production.
items.answer: (a) Diagram: MPB below MSB; MPC = MSC. Market output Q1 where MPB = MPC; optimum Q* where MSB = MSC is larger. Units between Q1 and Q* have MSB > MSC but are not consumed: welfare loss triangle between MSB and MSC from Q1 to Q*. (b) Diagram: price/cost on vertical axis, quantity horizontal. MPB = MSB downward sloping; MPC upward sloping; MSC above MPC by the marginal external cost. Market output Q1 where MPC = MSB; social optimum Q* where MSC = MSB, at a higher price. Between Q* and Q1, MSC > MSB: the triangle between MSC and MSB from Q* to Q1 is the deadweight welfare loss.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: MSB above MPB; 1 mark: Q1 < Q*; 1 mark: welfare loss triangle; 1 mark: reasoning [4] (b) 1 mark: correctly drawn curves; 1 mark: Q1 and Q*; 1 mark: identifies welfare loss area; 1 mark: explanation that MSC > MSB for those units [4]

items.stem: In the market for coal-fired electricity, MPB = MSB: P = 230 − 2Q and MPC: P = 30 + 2Q, where P is in $ and Q in thousand units. Production imposes a constant marginal external cost of $20. Calculate the free-market output and the socially optimal output.
items.answer: 50 thousand and 45 thousand

items.stem: In the market for plastic packaging, MPB = MSB: P = 150 − 2Q and MPC: P = 30 + 2Q, where P is in $ and Q in thousand units. Production imposes a constant marginal external cost of $16. Calculate the free-market output and the socially optimal output.
items.answer: 30 thousand and 26 thousand

items.stem: In the market for plastic packaging, MPB = MSB: P = 50 − 1Q and MPC: P = 10 + 1Q, where P is in $ and Q in thousand units. Production imposes a constant marginal external cost of $8. Calculate the free-market output and the socially optimal output.
items.answer: 20 thousand and 16 thousand

items.stem: A chemical works in Dhaka discharges waste into a river used by fishing communities. (a) With the aid of a diagram, explain how a negative production externality causes a misallocation of resources. (b) ‘Externalities provide the strongest case for government intervention in markets.’ Discuss this view.
items.answer: (a) Explanation of the theory (with a described diagram where relevant), drawing on: Externalities create welfare losses that markets cannot correct alone; taxes, subsidies, regulation. (b) Case for the view: Externalities create welfare losses that markets cannot correct alone; taxes, subsidies, regulation. Case against / evaluation: Other failures (public goods, monopoly, information) also justify intervention; government failure; measurement problems. Conclusion: a judgement on the conditions under which the view holds.
items.markingKey: (a) Knowledge and understanding of the theory, clear analytical chain; diagram described accurately with labelled axes and curves. (b) Analysis of arguments for and against; evaluation reaches a justified conclusion that weighs the conditions under which the claim holds. Top level needs a judgement, not just a summary.

items.stem: Vaccination rates in Ostrelia have fallen below the level needed to protect the whole population. Assess whether the welfare loss from positive externalities is less serious than that from negative externalities.
items.answer: Arguments for: Positive externalities: under-consumption, welfare loss triangle between MSB and MSC; negative: over-production and harm to third parties. Arguments against / evaluation: Size of loss depends on elasticities and size of externality, not its sign; education and vaccination losses can be large; long-run effects; equity aspects of who bears the cost. Conclusion: a supported judgement that depends on the conditions identified.
items.markingKey: Knowledge and analysis (about 60%): accurate theory, logical chains of reasoning and a relevant diagram described with axes, curves and shifts. Evaluation (about 40%): considers both sides, the assumptions and the context, and reaches a justified conclusion.

items.stem: Future costs and benefits in a CBA are discounted because
options: money received in the future is worth less than the same amount today
items.answer: money received in the future is worth less than the same amount today
items.markingKey: Time preference and opportunity cost of capital: PV = FV/(1 + r)ⁿ.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain how time savings from a new road might be valued in a cost-benefit analysis. (b) Explain two limitations of cost-benefit analysis.
items.answer: (a) By estimating hours saved per journey × number of journeys × a shadow price per hour (e.g. average wage for work time, a lower value for leisure). (b) Valuing intangibles (noise, lives, environment) relies on uncertain shadow prices; choice of discount rate can change the result; forecasting future benefits is uncertain; distribution of costs and benefits is ignored by a simple total.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: hours × journeys; 1 mark: shadow price per hour [2] (b) 1 mark each limitation identified, 1 mark each explained [4]

(b) Only units produced beyond the social optimum cause a net loss; external costs on units up to the optimum are outweighed by net benefits, so the welfare loss is the triangle, not the full area between MSC and MPC.

items.stem: The government of Quentara is appraising a light-rail line. The initial cost is $100m (now). Expected social benefits are $70m in year 1, $60m in year 2, $90m in year 3, with external costs of $10m each year. The discount rate is 6%. Calculate the present value of the net benefit in year 1.

The government of Nordavia is appraising a sports stadium. The initial cost is $250m (now). Expected social benefits are $60m in year 1, $100m in year 2, $100m in year 3, with external costs of $15m each year. The discount rate is 10%. Calculate the net present value and the benefit–cost ratio, and state whether the project should go ahead.
items.answer: NPV = −$74.98m; benefit–cost ratio = 0.7; reject on these figures.

items.stem: The government of Nordavia must choose between a new airport and a high-speed rail line. (a) Explain the stages involved in carrying out a cost-benefit analysis. (b) Discuss whether cost-benefit analysis is the best way for a government to decide whether to build a new transport project.
items.answer: (a) Explanation of the theory (with a described diagram where relevant), drawing on: CBA includes external effects, values them in money, discounts and compares, giving a consistent basis for decisions. (b) Case for the view: CBA includes external effects, values them in money, discounts and compares, giving a consistent basis for decisions. Case against / evaluation: Shadow pricing and forecasting uncertainty; discount rate choice; distributional effects ignored; political pressure; sensitivity analysis can help; other criteria (equity, environment) matter. Conclusion: a judgement on the conditions under which the view holds.
